chunks: First: Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Safwan and Fadala from Abd Allah ibn Sinan from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: 'God is not worshipped by anything more enduring than walking, nor is there anything superior.'

Second: Musa ibn al-Qasim from Ibn Abi Umayr from Hammad from al-Halabi said: 'I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the virtue of walking, so he said: Indeed, Al-Hasan ibn Ali (peace be upon him) made a pact with his Lord three times, until [he received] a pair of sandals, a pair of sandals, a garment, a garment, a dinar, a dinar, and [the reward of] Hajj for twenty pilgrimages, walking on his feet.'

Third: From him [Musa ibn al-Qasim] from Fadl ibn Amr from Muhammad ibn Ismail ibn Rajaa' al-Zabiri from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: 'God is not worshipped by anything superior to walking.'

Fourth: As for what Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa narrated from Al-Hasan ibn Ali from Rifa'a, who said: 'A man asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): Is riding superior or walking?' He said: 'Riding is superior to walking because the Messenger of God (peace be upon him) rode.'

Fifth: And what Musa ibn al-Qasim narrated from Ibn Abi Umayr from Saif al-Tammarr said: 'I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): It reached us that we were walking from you that year, and that you say regarding riding...' He said: 'Indeed, people perform Hajj walking and riding.' I said: 'I am not asking you about this.' He said: 'What are you asking me about?' I said: 'Which is more beloved to you, that we walk or ride?' He said: 'Riding is more beloved to me, for that is stronger for supplication and worship.'

Thus, the resolution between these two narrations is that whoever is strong in walking and is not weakened by it from supplication and rituals, or who has brought with him something to ride if exhausted, then walking is superior for him over riding. And whoever is weakened by walking and does not have what to resort to for riding when exhausted, then it is not permissible for him to depart except as a rider, according to what was explained in the narration.

And this meaning is also indicated by what Musa ibn al-Qasim narrated from Safwan from Abd Allah ibn Bukayr, who said: 'I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): We intend to depart to Mecca.' He said: 'Do not walk, but ride.' I said: 'May God perfect you, it reached us that Al-Hasan ibn Ali (peace be upon him) performed Hajj twenty times walking.' He said: 'Indeed, Al-Hasan ibn Ali (peace be upon him) would walk and his loads and beasts of burden would be driven with him. It is possible that he only preferred riding over walking when he knew that he would reach Mecca if he rode before the walkers, so he would worship God and increase in prayer until the walkers arrived.'

key_terms.الْحَسَنُ بْنُ عَلِيٍّ: Al-Hasan ibn Ali (peace be upon him)

ai.seo_question: Is walking or riding better for Hajj according to Shia hadith?
ai.summary: This passage from *Al-Istibsar* reconciles apparent contradictions in the Imams' preferences regarding Hajj travel by distinguishing between the spiritual merit of voluntary hardship (walking) and the practical necessity of preserving physical capacity for worship (riding). It highlights the Shia scholarly principle of *takhrij* (reconciliation), where the superiority of walking is conditional upon the pilgrim's ability to maintain devotion, while riding is preferred if it facilitates greater supplication or prevents exhaustion. The text also references the renowned practice of Imam al-Hasan ibn Ali, who walked while his baggage was carried, illustrating the ideal of combining physical effort with logistical ease.
